1. The present claim petition arises out of road accident that
occurred on 17.08.2019, in which the petitioner allegedly
suffered grievous injury. 
2.  The brief facts of the case are that on 17.08.2019,
petitioner alongwith his wife namely Sapna Sarkar was going from Anand Vihar, Delhi to Rudrapur, Uttrakhand by a roadways bus(Hapur depot) with registration number UP-14-DT-7758. 
When the said bus reached Chaudhrpur Pul, Amroha, U.P. at around 12.30 PM, another vehicle i.e. an open body truck bearing registration no. UP-23T-9324 (hereinafter referred to as the offending vehicle)came from the wrong side at a very high speed in a rash and negligent manner and hit the bus in which petitioner was travelling. As a result of collision between the two vehicles,
petitioner, alongwith other passengers fell off the bus and sustained grievous injuries. Petitioner and her wife were taken to the nearby hospital i.e. TMU hospital, Delhi Road, Muradabad,
U.P. and admitted for treatment. 
3. An FIR no. 344/2019 dated 17.08.2019 was registered u/s MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 2 Of 26 BK  :3:
279,337,338,427 of IPC at PS Didouli, Jyotiba Phule Nagar,
Amroha and the matter was investigated. After investigation a charge sheet was filed before Ld. MM.
4. Respondent no.1 is driver and Respondent no.2 is owner of the offending vehicle while Respondent no.3 is the insurance company with which such offending vehicle was insured. 
5. Despite service of summons through publication upon Respondent no.1 and Respondent no.2, they failed to appear before the court and did not enter any defence or filed any written statement. A reply was filed on behalf of Respondent no.3 as per which negligence or rashness on the part of the driver of offending vehicle has been denied and it is pleaded that the accident occurred due to sole negligence of the driver of the bus in which petitioner was travelling. It is further pleaded that the petition is bad for mis-joinder and non-joinder of necessary parties i.e. driver, owner and insurer of the bus in which petitioner was travelling. It has been pleaded that the Respondent no.3 can be held liable only if there was no violation of terms of the insurance policy or unless the driver held a valid licence and the owner of the offending vehicle held a valid Permit and fitness to ply the offending vehicle.

2 6. After completion of pleadings, following issues were framed on 15.12.2022.
 1. Whether the injured suffered injuries in a  road traffic accident on 17.08.2019 due to rash  and negligent driving of vehicle bearing  no.UP-23T-9324(truck) driven by R-1,owned  by R-2? OPP. 
 2. Whether the injured is entitled to any  compensation, if so, to what extent and from MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 3 Of 26 BK  :4:
 whom? OPP. 
 3. Relief.
7. Thereafter, evidence was led through local commissioner,
by the petitioner by examining petitioner Sh. Sushil Sarkar as PW-1. 
 PW-1/petitioner Sh. Sushil Sarkar led her evidence by way of affidavit Ex.PW1/A and relied upon her Aadhar card as Ex.PW-1/1, her treatment records as Ex.PW-1/2(colly), copy of FIR as Ex.PW-1/3, copy of driving licence of driver of offending vehicle as Ex.PW-1/4, copy of RC of offending vehicle as Ex.PW-1/5, certified copy of insurance policy of the offending vehicle as Ex.PW-1/6, certified copy of the site plan as Ex.PW- 1/7, certified copy of mechanical inspection report as Ex.PW-1/8,
certified copy of chargesheet as Ex.PW-1/9, certified copy of statement of petitioner/injured as Ex.PW-1/10 and copy of the bus ticket as Mark-A. PW-1 was duly cross examined by Ld. 
Counsel for Respondent no.3.
 Sh. Sushil Sarkar was examined as PW-2(inadvertently mentioned as PW-1). He tendered his evidence by way of affidavit as Ex.PW1/A(be read as Ex.PW-2/A). He relied upon his Aadhar card as Ex.PW-1/1(be read as Ex.PW-2/1), his treatment records as Ex.PW-1/2(colly)(be read as Ex.PW- 2/2(colly)) and copy of FIR, copy of driving licence of driver of offending vehicle, copy of RC of offending vehicle, certified copy of insurance policy of the offending vehicle, certified copy of the site plan, certified copy of mechanical inspection report,
certified copy of chargesheet as already exhibited in the evidence of PW-1 as Ex.PW-1/3 to PW-1/11(be read as Ex.PW-2/11),
MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 4 Of 26 BK  :5:
original disability certificate as Ex.PW-1/12(be read as Ex.PW- 2/12), copy of statement of eye witness as Ex.PW-1/13(be read as Ex.PW-2/13) and copy of bus ticket as Ex.PW-1/14(be read as Ex.PW-2/14). He was duly cross- examined by Ld. Counsel for Respondent no.3.
8. Respondent no.3 also led evidence by examining one Sh.
Rahul Verma as R-3W-1 and Sh. R.V. Singh, Surveyor as R-3W- Sushil Kumar vs Rafeeuddin on 24 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/166521476/
3 2. R-3W-1 tendered his evidence by way of affidavit as Ex.R- 3W-1/1 and relied upon Power of Attorney/authorization as Ex.R-3W-1/2, attested insurance policy as Ex.R-3W-1/3,
investigation report of fitness as Mark-A and notices served under Order XII Rule 8 CPC alongwith receipts as Ex.R-3W- 1/5(colly). The witness was not cross-examined despite opportunity. 
 R-3W-2 Sh. R.V. Singh, Surveyor R-3W-1 tendered his evidence by way of affidavit as Ex.R-3W-2/1 and relied upon online fitness verification report as Ex.R-3W-2/1 alongwith a certificate u/s 65-B of Indian Evidence Act. He was not cross- examined despite opportunity given. 
9. Final arguments in details were addressed by all the parties. On the basis of pleadings of the parties, evidence adduced and arguments addressed, issue wise findings are as under:
 Issue No. 1  Whether the injured suffered injuries in a road  traffic accident on 17.08.2019 due to rash and  negligent driving of vehicle bearing no.UP-  23T-9324(truck) driven by R-1,owned by R-2?
 OPP.
MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 5 Of 26 BK  :6:
10. Before proceeding to decide the above issue, it is apposite to note that as a settled principle of law, proceedings under The Motor Vehicle Act are not considered akin to the proceedings in a civil suit and hence strict rules of evidence are not applicable.
Reliance is placed upon decision in Bimla Devi & ors. vs.
Himachal Road Transport Corporation & ors. (2009) 13 SC 535, in Parmeshwari vs. Amir Chand & ors., 2011 (1) SCR 1096 and National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana,
2009 ACJ 287, wherein it has been held that the negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view has to be taken. 
11. In the present case, petitioner/injured has been examined as PW-1 wherein he has deposed that on 17.08.2019, he alongwith his wife namely Sapna Sarkar was travelling by a Roadways bus bearing registration UP-14DT-7758 and that at around 12.30 pm, the offending vehicle i.e. a goods carrier truck bearing no. UP23T-9324 suddenly came from wrong side at a high speed in a rash and negligent manner and hit the bus in which petitioner was travelling due to which petitioner fell down and suffered grievous injuries. PW-1 further deposed that he was taken TMU hospital for treatment from where he was later shifted to Safderjung hospital. He has deposed that due to the accident, he received injuries on head, face(jaw), legs and multiple injuries all over his body. 
 During the cross-examination, PW-1 deposed that at the time of accident, all passengers were seated. He deposed that the accident took place on a three-way lane road meaning thereby Sushil Kumar vs Rafeeuddin on 24 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/166521476/
4 that three vehicles could ply on each side of the road. He MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 6 Of 26 BK  :7:
testified that there was a divider and that the traffic on the road was moderate at the time of accident. Hhe further deposed that in her cross-examination that the bus that she was travelling in was plying in the right most lane next to the divider while the offending truck came from the front side. A suggestion has been put to PW-1 as to negligence of the bus driver of the bus in which petitioner was travelling, which has been denied. There is no suggestion that the offending vehicle was being plied in a wrong direction in violation to the traffic norms. In these circumstances,
even if the bus was being driven at a high speed, same would not tantamount to contributory negligence on the part of the bus driver when the accident has occurred due to collision with the offending truck being driven in the opposite direction against the traffic rules. 
 Although a defence that the bus was overloaded with passengers or that it was being driven at a high speed due to which it lost control has been denied by both the petitioner's witnesses, no evidence has been brought forth by the respondents to prove such a plea. Hence, no contributory negligence has been proved on the part of the driver of the bus in which petitioner was travelling. This also defeats the plea of the petition being bad in law due to non-joinder of necessary parties. 
12. Facts and the evidence led, makes it abundantly evident that the accident was caused due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle. In the present case, police after investigation had filed charge sheet against Respondent no.1 under Section 279,337,338,427 of IPC which is also suggestive of negligence of respondent in causing the accident. The IO has MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 7 Of 26 BK  :8:
filed Detailed Accident Report before this Tribunal. In National Insurance Co. vs. Pushpa Rana 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi, it was laid down that completion of investigation and filing of charge sheet are sufficient proof of negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle. 
13. Neither the driver nor the owner of the offending vehicle have entered into the witness box or raised any defence. 
14. It may further be noted that in Cholamandlam insurance company Ltd. Vs. Kamlesh 2009 (3) AD Delhi 310, it was held that if driver of offending vehicle does not enter the witness box,
an adverse inference can be drawn against him. In the present case also, driver did not enter into the witness box to controvert the claim of petitioner or even to explain circumstances of accident. 
15. On perusal of examination-in-chief by way of affidavit of PW-1, it is noted that PW-1/Petitioner deposed on the lines of Sushil Kumar vs Rafeeuddin on 24 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/166521476/
5 petitioner's original stand as already noted above. It was further deposed that due to rash and negligent driving of the R-1, the accident in question took place. Further, even the medical documents support the claimant that injuries caused in road accident. 
16. In totality of circumstances, this Tribunal is of the opinion that the claimant have been able to prove at the scales of preponement of probabilities that the accident in question, took place due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle by its driver/respondent no.1 on the date and time of accident. 
Accordingly, issue no.1 is decided in favour of petitioner/
claimant/applicant and against the respondents.
MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 8 Of 26 BK  :9:
 Issue no. 2  Whether the injured is entitled to any  compensation, if so, to what extent and from  whom? OPP. 
17. Respondent no.3 has examined R-3W-1 Sh. Rahul Verma,
Assistant Manager of Respondent no.3 to prove that the liability of the insurance company is subject to terms and conditions of the insurance policy and that, as per the investigation report, the owner did not possess a valid and effective fitness of the offending vehicle at the time of accident and thereby committed a fundamental breach of the terms and conditions of the insurance policy. 
 Further, R-3W-2 Sh. R.V. Singh, Surveyor-cum- investigator was examined to prove that the fitness of the offending vehicle was valid from 11.07.2018 till 10.07.2019 and was renewed on 24.01.2020 to 23.01.2022. As none of the respondent's witnesses have been cross- examined, it stands proved that the offending vehicle did not possess fitness validity on 17.08.2019. 
 Since Respondent no.3 has disowned the liability to compensate the petitioner on the ground that the offending vehicle did not have a valid fitness certificate for being plied on the road, the issue is being dealt in the light of decision of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Kaushalpati Pandey v. New India Assurance Co. Ltd. (decided on 09.11.2020). In that case, a similar issue was under consideration regarding the recovery rights to the insurance company in case of no fitness certificate as on the date of accident. The court cited the following observation of Hon'ble Kerala High Court made in Ramankutty v. Pareed MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 9 Of 26 BK  : 10 :
Pillai 2018 SCC Online Ker 3542:
 "...18.The stipulations under the above provisions clearly  substantiate the importance and necessity to have a valid  Fitness Certificate to the transport vehicle at all times. The Sushil Kumar vs Rafeeuddin on 24 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/166521476/
6  above prescription converges on the point that Certificate of  Registration, existence of valid Permit and availability of  Fitness Certificate, all throughout, are closely Interlinked In  the case of a transport vehicle and one requirement cannot  be segregated from the other. The transport vehicle should  be completely fit and road worthy, to be plied on the road,
 which otherwise may cause threat to the lives and limbs of  passengers and the general public, apart from damage to  property. Only If the transport vehicle is having valid  Fitness Certificate, would the necessary Permit be issued In  terms of Section 66 of the Act and by virtue of the mandate  under Section 56 of the Act, no transport vehicle without  Fitness Certificate will be deemed as a validly registered  vehicle for the purpose of Section 39 of the Act, which  stipulates that nobody shall drive or cause the motor vehicle  to be driven without valid registration in public place or  such other place, as the case may be. These requirements  are quite fundamental in nature; unlike a case where a  transport vehicle carrying more passengers than the  permitted capacity or a goods carriage carrying excess  quantity of goods than the permitted extent or a case where  a transport vehicle was plying through a deviated route than  the one shown in the route permit which instances could  rather be branded as technical violations. In other words,
 when a transport vehicle is not having a Fitness Certificate,
 it will be deemed as having no Certificate of Registration  and when such vehicle is not having Permit or Fitness  Certificate, nobody can drive such vehicle and no owner  can permit the use of any such vehicle compromising with  the lives. limbs, properties of the passengers/general public. 
 Obviously, since the safety of passengers and general public  was of serious concern and consideration for the law  makers, appropriate and adequate measures were taken by  incorporating relevant provisions in the Statute, also  pointing out the circumstances which would constitute  offence; providing adequate penalty. This being the  position, such lapse, if any, can only be regarded as a  fundamental breach and not a technical breach and any  interpretation to the contrary, will only negate the intention  of the law makers. 
 .... 
22. The question whether absence of valid Permit to a transport vehicle at the time of accident is a fundamental MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 10 Of 26 BK breach or a technical breach had come up for consideration again before the Apex Court recently in Amrit paul Singh v. TATA AIG General Insurance Co. Ltd., [2018 (3) KHC 197]. The factual matrix in the said case is that, the rider of the motor cycle was knocked down to death by the offending truck on 19.02.2013, which led to the claim petition preferred by the legal heirs. The claim was resisted by the insurer, mainly contending that there was violation of policy conditions in so far as the offending truck was not having a valid Permit and the driver was not having a valid driving licence. Based on the materials on record and placing reliance on the verdict passed by the Apex Court in Challa Sushil Kumar vs Rafeeuddin on 24 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/166521476/
7 Upendra Rao's case [cited supra], the Tribunal, after fixing the quantum of compensation, directed the insurer to satisf the same, with liberty to have it recovered from the insured. The said finding and reasoning came to be affirmed by the High Court, in turn leading to the proceedings before the Apex Court. After exhaustive discussion on the relevant provisions of law including Section 2(28),
2(31), 2(47), 66, 149 and 166 of the M.V. Act 1988 and the various judgments rendered by the Apex Court at different points of time, including in National Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Swaran Singh [(2004) 3 SCC 297] and Challa Upendra Rao's case [cited supra], the Apex Court held that the offending truck was not having a valid Permit on the date of accident; which was not a technical breach to attract the dictum in Swaran Singhs' case [cited supra] [where also right of recovery was held as conferred on the insurer, once the breach was established by the insurer]. It was also observed that, it was not a case where any of the exceptions under sub-section (3) of Section 66 was attracted and further that,
existence of a Permit of any nature was matter of documentary evidence. The Bench held that the exceptions carved out under Section 66(3) of the Act are to be pleaded and proved by the insured/owner and this burden cannot be shifted to the shoulders of the insurer. It has accordingly been declared that, the use of a transport vehicle in a public place without Permit is a fundamental/statutory infraction and the principles laid down in Swaran Singh's case [cited supra]
and Lakshmi Chand v. Reliance General Insurance [(2016) 3 SCC 100] cannot be applicable in this regard. The Apex Court held, in such circumstances, that the verdict passed by the High Court affirming the stand of the Tribunal directing the insurer to satisfy the liability and to have it recovered from the owner/insured was in consonance with the principles stated in Swaran Singh's case [cited supra] and other cases pertaining to pay and recover principle. From the above, it is quite evident that the law stands settled by the Apex MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 11 Of 26 BK Court as per the decision Challa Upendra Rao' case [cited supra] and the latest ruling in Amrit paul's case [cited supra]. This being the position, the dictum laid down by the Full Bench of this Court in Augustine V.M. v. Ayyappankutty @ Mani [cited supra] holding that the absence of valid Permit or Fitness Certificate is not a fundamental breach, but a technical breach and that no right of recovery can be given to the insurer is not at all correct. It accordingly stands overruled. Consequently, the dictum in Tharas case [cited supra] is restored and the contrary view expressed in Sethunaths case [cited supra] stands declared as incorrect." 
Hon'ble Delhi High Court further held in Kaushalpati case (supra) that the obvious rational for a valid fitness certificate is the proof that the vehicle is working properly apropos all vital aspects i.e.,
its brakes, indicator lights, wipers, seat-belts, etc. are working optimally, so that the vehicle can be manoeuvred on a public street without causing damage to anybody. If there is default in any of these requisite conditions, then the vehicle itself would be a danger to public safety and would impose a traffic hazard. 
18. In view of the observation, the compensation shall be payable to the petitioner/injured by the insurance company of offending vehicle bearing registration number UP-23T-9324 and then the insurance company shall be entitled to recover the same from the driver and the owner of the offending vehicle. 
19. As regards the quantum of compensation, this court is governed by the law laid down by Hon'le Supreme Court in Raj Kumar Vs. Ajay Kumar & Anr. (2011) 1 Supreme Court cases 343, Sarla Verma Sushil Kumar vs Rafeeuddin on 24 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/166521476/
8 & Ors. v. Delhi Transport Corporation & Ors. (2003) 6SCC 121 and National Insurance Company Limited v. Pranay Sethi & Ors.(2017) 16 SCC 680. 
MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 12 Of 26 BK The gist of the law is that the object of awarding damages is to make good the loss suffered as a result of wrong done as far as money can do so, in a fair, reasonable and equitable manner. The court or the Tribunal shall have to assess the damages objectively and exclude from consideration any speculation or fancy, though some conjecture with reference to the nature of disability and its consequences, is inevitable. A person is not only to be compensated for the physical injury, but also for the loss which he suffered as a result of such injury. This means that he is to be compensated for his inability to lead a full life,
his inability to enjoy those normal amenities which he would have enjoyed but for the injuries, and his inability to earn as much as he used to earn or could have earned.
20. Further it can be noted that the heads under which compensation is awarded in personal injury cases are the following:
Pecuniary damages (Special damages)
(i) Expenses relating to treatment, hospitalisation, medicines, transportation,
nourishing food, and miscellaneous expenditure.
(ii) Loss of earnings (and other gains) which the injured would have made had he not been injured, comprising:
(a) Loss of earning during the period of treatment;
(b) Loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability.
(iii) Future medical expenses. 
Non-pecuniary damages (General damages)
(iv) Damages for pain, suffering and trauma as a MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v.
Rafeeuddin P.No. 13 Of 26 BK consequence of the injuries. 
(v) Loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage).
(vi) Loss of expectation of life (shortening of normal longevity).
20.1. In routine personal injury cases, compensation will be awarded only under heads (i), (ii) (a)
and (iv). 20.2. It is only in serious cases of injury, where there is specific medical evidence corroborating the evidence of the claimant, that compensation will be granted under any of the heads (ii)(b), (iii),
Sushil Kumar vs Rafeeuddin on 24 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/166521476/
9 (v) and (vi) relating to loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability, future medical expenses, loss of amenities (and/or loss of prospects of marriage) and loss of expectation of life.
20.3. Assessment of pecuniary damages under Item (i) and under Item (ii) (a) do not pose much difficulty as they involve reimbursement of actuals and are easily ascertainable from the evidence.
20.4. Award under the head of future medical expenses--Item (iii)--depends upon specific medical evidence regarding need for further treatment and cost thereof. 
20.5. Assessment of non-pecuniary damages--Items (iv), (v) and (vi)--involves determination of l u m p s u m a m o u n t s w i t h r e f e r e n c e t o c i r c u m s t a n c e s s u c h a s a g e , n a t u r e o f injury/deprivation/disability suffered by the claimant and the effect thereof on the future life of the claimant. Decisions of Hon'ble SC and Hon'ble High Courts contain necessary guidelines for award under these heads, if necessary. 
MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 14 Of 26 BK 20.6. It was observed by Hon'ble Sc in such case of Raj Kumar (supra) that what usually poses some difficulty is the assessment of the loss of future earnings on account of permanent disability--Item (ii) (a).
21. In the present case, petitioner has claimed permanent disability on account of the injuries suffered in the accident. As per the disability certificate Ex.PW-1/12, petitioner has been assessed to be suffering from 21% permanent disability in relation to his right upper limb. A defence has been raised by Ld. Counsel for insurance company that this disability is a pre- existent disability which did not subsequently occurred due to the accident. In order to appreciate this argument, this court has gone through the medical treatment papers prepared at TMU hospital where the petitioner was first treated as well as the medical record of Safderjung hospital where he was subsequently shifted.
As per the noting of the doctor on the discharge summary of Safderjung hospital, the petitioner was referred to get examined for fracture in his lower limb. Apart from mere pain and swelling found around right wrist, no apparent injury is seen on his upper limb. The OPD card specifically mentions the injury suffered as wound in knee. There is no medical document showing that the petitioner suffered any grievous injury in his upper limb so as to lead to permanent disability. Thus, the disability does not appear to have any co-relation or nexus with the injuries suffered in the accident and therefore, the present case cannot be categorized as a case of permanent disability. 
Further, despite referral of the petitioner for being examined to detect fracture, no X-ray report or any other medical MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 15 Of 26 BK document has been filed. Documents however reveal that petitioner suffered head injury and had referred to neurological department but there is no assessment of the neurological treatment or injury suffered. 
However, as the petitioner remained hospitalized for three days, injuries can be assumed to be grievous in nature. 
22. The age of petitioner is not disputed. As per Ex.PW-1/1 Aadhar card, the year of birth is shown to be 1961 and as such, the injured/petitioner would have been around 58 years of age. 
Sushil Kumar vs Rafeeuddin on 24 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/166521476/
10 Ex.PW-1/2(colly) are his medical treatment papers which show that at the time of such treatment injured had alleged road traffic accident. Though, no formal MLC is on record, there is nothing to doubt the medical treatment papers including OPD record of Safderjung hospital, New Delhi showing that the injured suffered pain,swelling, wound below knee and pain and swelling around right wrist. 
The medical treatment papers relied upon by the petitioner shows that he remained hospitalized from 17.08.2019 at 12 PM to 19.08.2019 till 10.30 PM and as such keeping in view the nature of injury; the fact that though it has not been proved that petitioner could not carry on his daily pursuits or was rendered incapable of working but assuming that it may have taken about one month to completely recover from the injuries sustained; the fact that no salary or income proof has been filed and thus assessment of his income has to be as per minimum wages of unskilled labour prevalent in Uttarakhand, compensation under the head of loss of income would be Rs.9772/-.
The bills placed on record prove an expenditure of MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 16 Of 26 BK Rs.89,193/-.

 the bills placed on record. 
 (ii) Expenditure on Conveyance : The Rs.5,000/-

 Thus, having regard to the fact that petitioner remained hospitalized for 3 days and did not return to take further treatment, by guesswork, compensation can be awarded for conveyance. 
(iii) Expenditure on special diet : The Rs.10,000/-
petitioner has not filed any bill or prescription for special diet. 
The nature of injuries are grievous. 
Therefore, having regard to the nature of injury and the treatment, by guess work, compensation can be awarded for special diet. 
(iv) Cost of nursing / attendant : The 10,000/- petitioner has not filed any bill or prescription for nursing/ attendant charges. Even in the absence of documentary proof, compensation for Sushil Kumar vs Rafeeuddin on 24 April, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/166521476/

 shock: As the petitioner has suffered  grievous injuries, he would have  undergone mental and physical shock.

summary.ANALYSIS:
Before proceeding to decide the above issue, it is apposite to note that as a settled principle of law, proceedings under The Motor Vehicle Act are not considered akin to the proceedings in a civil suit and hence strict rules of evidence are not applicable.
Reliance
(2009) 13 SC 535, in Parmeshwari vs. Amir Chand & ors., 2011 (1) SCR 1096 and National Insurance Company Ltd. vs. Pushpa Rana,
2009 ACJ 287, wherein it has been held that the negligence has to be decided on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities and a holistic view has to be taken.
There is no suggestion that the offending vehicle was being plied in a wrong direction in violation to the traffic norms.
In these circumstances,
even if the bus was being driven at a high speed, same would not tantamount to contributory negligence on the part of the bus driver when the accident has occurred due to collision with the offending truck being driven in the opposite direction against the traffic rules.

 Although a defence that the bus was overloaded with passengers or that it was being driven at a high speed due to which it lost control has been denied by both the petitioner's witnesses, no evidence has been brought forth by the respondents to prove such a plea.
Hence, no contributory negligence has been proved on the part of the driver of the bus in which petitioner was travelling.
This also defeats the plea of the petition being bad in law due to non-joinder of necessary parties.

12. Facts and the evidence led, makes it abundantly evident that the accident was caused due to rash and negligent driving of the offending vehicle.
In the present case, police after investigation had filed charge sheet against Respondent no.1 under Section 279,337,338,427 of IPC which is also suggestive of negligence of respondent in causing the accident.
The IO has MACT NO: 68/20 Sushil Sarkar v. Rafeeuddin P.No. 7 Of 26 BK  :8:
filed Detailed Accident Report before this Tribunal.
In National Insurance Co. vs. Pushpa Rana 2009 ACJ 287 Delhi, it was laid down that completion of investigation and filing of charge sheet are sufficient proof of negligence of the driver of the offending vehicle.
These requirements  are quite fundamental in nature; unlike a case where a  transport vehicle carrying more passengers than the  permitted capacity or a goods carriage carrying excess  quantity of goods than the permitted extent or a case where  a transport vehicle was plying through a deviated route than  the one shown in the route permit which instances could  rather be branded as technical violations.
In other words,
 when a transport vehicle is not having a Fitness Certificate,
 it will be deemed as having no Certificate of Registration  and when such vehicle is not having Permit or Fitness  Certificate, nobody can drive such vehicle and no owner  can permit the use of any such vehicle compromising with  the lives.
limbs, properties of the passengers/general public.

 Obviously, since the safety of passengers and general public  was of serious concern and consideration for the law  makers, appropriate and adequate measures were taken by  incorporating relevant provisions in the Statute, also  pointing out the circumstances which would constitute  offence; providing adequate penalty.
This being the  position, such lapse, if any, can only be regarded as a  fundamental breach and not a technical breach and any  interpretation to the contrary, will only negate the intention  of the law makers.

the Tribunal is satisfied for reasons to be stated in writing that the whole or part of the amount is required for expanding an existing business or for purchasing some property for earning a livelihood, the Tribunal can release the whole or part of the amount of compensation to the claimant provided the Tribunal will ensure that the amount is invested for the purpose for which it is demanded and paid.
